papers.title: TeamLearn: A Multimodal, AI-enhanced Dashboard for Reflection During Collaborative Problem-Solving
papers.authors: Rogers Kaliisa, Crina Damşa, Jan Arild Dolonen, Malcolm Langford, Runar Hilleren Lie, Terje Kristian Lian Thoresen, Richard Nesnass, Krishna Siddharth Rajasekaran

papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners
papers.abstract: This demo presents TeamLearn, a multimodal collaboration analytics dashboard designed to facilitate reflection and provide feedback on developing group artifacts during long- term collaborative problem-solving projects. By integrating meetings, documents, and collaboration experience analytics, the dashboard offers visualisations that help groups monitor participation, task progress, and collaboration dynamics. Developed through a design-based research process, the TeamLearn dashboard provides structured opportunities for reflective dialogue. The demo will showcase the dashboard’s core features and illustrate how it can be integrated into collaborative project activities.

papers.authors: Dina Samson, Jonan Phillip Donaldson
papers.teacher_involvement: **Involvement**: Teachers actively participated in collaborative co-design workshops, design meetings, or teacher communities with researchers to iteratively develop, test, and adapt curriculum units, assessments, and lesson plans. **Evidence**: "For instance, the instructor could engage students in co-designing a low-stakes activity early in the design process that is intended to result in failure."
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This design-based research study investigated student experiences in a co- designed, asynchronous online graduate course. We applied learning experience network analysis to examine 43 student reflection papers. The analysis identified seven distinct learning ecologies, each characterized by different configurations of learner agency, theoretical principles, and challenges. While two ecologies represented successful engagement, five others revealed specific struggles. These struggles included translating individual work into group collaboration and managing anxiety during transformative learning. This study shows that co-design resulted in varied learning ecologies of experiences. We proposed specific design moves for each challenging configuration. Network analysis offered a valuable method for systematically improving co-designed learning environments through responsive, theory-based support.

papers.design_stakeholders: Special Education Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: As the Learning Sciences have continued discussing subtle nuances related to community partnerships, there has been emphasis on how to enact solidarity, healing, and care. In this piece, we reflect on our enactments of solidarity and care by sharing about moments of calling-in, which we refer to as moments of curiously challenging. We use examples from our co-design sessions to showcase how call -ins function as transformative disruptions of harmful knowledges and how these moments are situated within other relationship building practices. We call on other scholars within the Learning Sciences community to consider the complexities surrounding systemized mindsets and how to attend to harmful productions and reproductions of knowledge within community-based partnerships.

papers.title: Learning With and About AI: Building Capacity for Equitable Participation in an AI-Shaped Future
papers.authors: Ibrahim Oluwajoba Adisa
papers.teacher_involvement: **Involvement**: Teachers actively participated in collaborative co-design workshops, design meetings, or teacher communities with researchers to iteratively develop, test, and adapt curriculum units, assessments, and lesson plans. **Evidence**: "I employ design-based research to iteratively co-design data science and AI resources with educators and community partners, while developing mid-level theoretical constructs regarding AI literacy and learner–AI collaboration."
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: My research investigates how learners and educators understand, design with, and collaborate with AI systems, and how these sociotechnical interactions shape equity and participation. Using design-based research, participatory design, and qualitative and computational methods, I study AI education and disciplinary integration of AI in K–12 contexts. My work aims to design equitable learning environments, develop theoretical models of learner engagement with AI, and build cross-disciplinary approaches to teaching with and about AI. Theoretical and methodological foundations that inform my work My research sits at the intersection of the learning sciences, data science and artificial intelligence (AI) education. I am particularly interested in how educators and learners understand, design with, and collaborate with AI systems, and how these sociotechnical interactions shape equity and participation in society. In my work, I frame learning as a socially and materially mediated practice, drawing on sociocultural perspectives that conceptualize knowing as participation in activity systems rather than simply the acquisition of decontextualized concepts (Vygotsky, 1987; Wertsch, 1991). Within this view, AI tools and data infrastructures function as cultural tools (Cole, 1996; Saxe, 1991) that shape what becomes visible, what is considered authoritative, and whose perspectives are deemed valid as knowledge. I also draw on constructionist (Holbert et al., 2020; Kafai & Resnick, 1996; Papert & Harel, 1991) and design-oriented traditions that treat building computational artifacts as a powerful avenue for learning. When students build or critique AI applications and data stories, they are engaging in epistemic work that reveals their assumptions about what counts as evidence, how models relate to the world, and whose experiences are encoded in data (Vakil et al., 2022). I am particularly attentive to how young learners develop both conceptual and sociotechnical understandings of the affordances and limits of AI technologies, and how educators can support these competencies in ways that foster agency, critique, and creativity.

papers.title: Frame Alignment and Feedback in CT-ified Science Classrooms
papers.authors: Connor Bain, Uri Wilensky
papers.teacher_involvement: **Involvement**: Teachers partnered with researchers in an iterative collaborative design process to conceptualize, author, and contextualize curricular materials and learning activities tailored to their classroom environments. **Evidence**: "We report on the efforts of a design-based implementation research project in which teachers participate in a constructionist co-design process to design and then implement CT -ified STEM units in their classrooms."
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: While computational thinking (CT) is an integral part of modern scientific inquiry, STEM teachers struggle to incorporate these ideas in classrooms. We report on the efforts of a design-based implementation research project in which teachers participate in a constructionist co-design process to design and then implement CT -ified STEM units in their classrooms. Using feedback teachers left on student responses from these unit implementations, we utilize a basic bag-of-words model to show that teachers did specifically attend to student learning at the intersection of CT and STEM. We then further explicate this evidence through a qualitative think-aloud interview with one of the teachers who designed and implemented a curriculum based around computational models in biology. What we find is evidence that STEM teachers in CT -ified classrooms can assess both CT and S TEM skills at the same time though this intersection still needs additional attention in terms of tools and PD for teachers.

papers.abstract: In this practice -oriented paper, we underscore ICLS’s 2026 theme of “Partnering with Purpose” by describing the process and outcomes of a collaborative project between community members and a large public university. By attending to values of reciprocity, relationships, community expertise, and the power of place, we developed a set of curriculum materials that draw on the expertise of two Black urban farmers in their work to transform educational and agricultural experiences for youth. We outline our collaborative process, project outcomes, and next steps for supporting this and other innovative community partnerships.

Educators can structure design review sessions where teams use AR to present their work, with peers providing feedback while viewing the..."

papers.abstract: This study aims to explore the affordances of augmented reality technologies (AR) to facilitate studentsʼ product design processes in a business course. We analyze the affordances of AR in the context of a product design activity in an undergraduate classroom. The course is held in a Makerspace lab at a university campus, and it requires students to conceptualize, design, prototype, manufacture, and market new products by using 3D computer -aided design (CAD) software and 3D printing. Our study illuminates that although CAD allows students to visualize and manipulate digitally manufactured 3D objects on a 2D computer monitor surface, it does not allow them to visualize and manipulate those 3D objects in 3D space. However, AR does afford visualization and mani pulation of digitally manufactured 3D objects in 3D space which is why we investigated how do interactions with 3D models in AR impact product design processes for students.

papers.title: Teacher as Designers: Using Robotics to Integrate Computational Thinking and Science
papers.authors: Michael Cassidy, Debra Bernstein, Jennifer Cross, Karen Mutch-Jones
papers.teacher_involvement: **Involvement**: Teachers actively participated in collaborative co-design workshops, design meetings, or teacher communities with researchers to iteratively develop, test, and adapt curriculum units, assessments, and lesson plans. **Evidence**: "Professional development that supports this role emphasizes strategies such as active learning, practice- based inquiry, and collaborative design, which create opportunities for teachers to engage directly with new ideas while situating them in the realities of classroom pract..."
papers.design_stakeholders: Middle School Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This study examines how middle school science teachers designed and implemented robotics-based units that integrated computational thinking (CT) practices following a professional development (PD) program positioning them as curriculum designers. Drawing on Waterman et al.’s (2020) and Coenraad et al.’s (2022) integration frameworks and the project’s CT framework (Bernstein et al., 2025 ), we analyzed teacher interviews, implementation logs, lesson plans, and student materials from six teachers across twelve units. Findings show that teachers implemented CT at multiple integration levels, engaging students in algorithm design, decomposition, abstraction, pattern recognition, and data practices. Teachers explored CT practices to establish foundational understanding, enhanced CT– science connections through scaffolds, and guided students to exhibit disciplinary ideas through programmable mode ls and extend understanding by collecting and analyzing data. These findings illustrate how positioning teachers as informed designers supports CT-integrated science curricula. Importance Computational technologies are essential for problem solving and collaboration in both professional and personal contexts (NRC, 2014). In STEM fields, these technologies have transformed practice through abstraction, algorithms, decomposition, modeling, simulation, and data analysis enabled by computing (Puttick et al., 2024; Weintrop et al., 2016). Preparing students to participate in such transformations requires the development of computational thinking (CT) practices, defined as “solving problems, designing systems, and understanding human behavior, by drawing on the concepts fundamental to computer science” (Wing, 2006, p. 33). Such preparation positions students to become producers, not merely consumers, of computational solutions. Yet despite growing calls to integrate CT into K –12 science classrooms, teachers face persistent challenges in designing learning tasks where CT meaningfully supports science learning (Cassidy & Puttick , 2022). Teachers are rarely positioned as designers of curricula that combine science, engineering, and computing (Margot & Kettler, 2019), leaving limited evidence on how to support them in planning, adapting, and enacting such curricula in authentic ways (Lee et al., 2020). Conceptual framework Computational Thinking (CT) Prior research offers important frameworks for conceptualizing CT integration. For example, Waterman et al. (2020) introduced a continuum of CT integration in science education, distinguishing between levels where CT exists (CT concepts, skills, and practices already present in the lesson can be called out or elaborated upon by the teacher, often without technology use), enhances (development of additional tasks or lessons that serve to deepen the disciplinary concept while making explicit connections to relevant computing ideas), and extends (redesign or expand lessons so that computing or CT practices become central to students’ engagement with disciplinary content). More recently, Coenraad et al. (2022) added the category of exhibit, which emphasizes students’ representing science knowledge through computational models. These frameworks provide a robust lens for describing the variety of ways CT can interact with disciplinary science learning. Engaging with robotics enables learners to develop CT practices while investigating core scientific phenomena, positioning robotics as a powerful context for integrating disciplinary learning with computational problem solving (Cassidy & Puttick, 2022). Through robotics, students apply key CT practices such as problem decomposition, abstraction, algorithmic design, and iterative debugging. These activities also support engagement in core science practices, including modeling, experimentation, and data collection and analysis (e.g., Sullivan & Hefernan, 2016). For the Robots in Science project, we adopted the PRADA framework (Dong et al., 2019), which emphasizes pattern recognition, abstraction, decomposition, and algorithms. To better align with the needs of 1297 science and robotics integration, we extended PRADA by including a fifth practice, Data Practices (Weintrop et al., 2016). In our framework, pattern recognition refers to identifying similarities among and within problems. Abstraction involves stripping away unnecessary details to develop a generic solution or representing a complex system through a simplified model or visualization. Decomposition is the process of breaking down data, processes, or problems into smaller, manageable parts. Algorithm design c oncerns the creation of an ordered sequence of instructions to solve a problem or perform a task. Data practices include collecting information, analyzing it to generate insights, and representing it through graphs, charts, words, or images. Professional development for teachers-as-designers Positioning teachers as designers acknowledges their capabilities as effective curriculum developers who draw on both disciplinary knowledge and classroom expertise (Penuel & Gallagher, 2009). This approach recognizes teachers’ pedagogical knowledge, their professional judgment, and their ability to innovate in response to their unique contexts (Voogt et al., 2019). When teachers design and/or adapt their curricula and instructional practices, they put disciplinary goals, student learning needs, and classroom resources at the forefront of implementation (Puttick et al. , 2025). Professional development that supports this role emphasizes strategies such as active learning, practice- based inquiry, and collaborative design, which create opportunities for teachers to engage directly with new ideas while situating them in the realities of classroom practice (Darling -Hammond, 2017; Tucker-Raymond & Gravel, 2019). Also, time is needed to be allotted for deep play with new technologies and resources (Koehler et al., 2011). Thus, teachers’ curriculum adaptations are shaped by their wisdom of practice and responsiveness to student needs (Calabrese Barton et al., 2021).

papers.title: “It’s aligned with my personal beliefs, i can do this”: How Science Educators Navigate Tensions Between Official and Counter Scripts of Science and Learning
papers.authors: Shaghig Chaparian, Olivia Ortiz, Maia Yoshida, Kam Waugh, Jasmine Ma, Ronni Hayden, Latasha Wright
papers.teacher_involvement: **Involvement**: Teachers actively participated in collaborative co-design workshops, design meetings, or teacher communities with researchers to iteratively develop, test, and adapt curriculum units, assessments, and lesson plans. **Evidence**: "Findings reveal that educators mobilize personal histories to create hybrid pedagogical spaces emphasizing freedom, flexibility, and epistemic justice. These third-space negotiations obscure boundaries between scientific and community knowledge, transforming science into a rel..."
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This study examines how informal science educators transform their lived experiences of migration, activism, and encounters with marginalization into pedagogical commitments focused on social justice. Drawing on Holland and Lave’s history-in-person and Gutiérrez’s third-space concepts, we explore how educators’ histories serve as mediational resources that shape teaching philosophies and reconfigure who belongs in science. Using semi- structured interviews with community scientists from Daphnia , an after -school science organization serving marginalized youth, the analysis traces how educators navigated and re - authored official and unofficial scripts about legitimate science and participation. Findings reveal that educators mobilize personal histories to create hybrid pedagogical spaces emphasizing freedom, flexibility, and epistemic justice. These third-space negotiations obscure boundaries between scientific and community knowledge, transforming science into a relational, participatory practice rooted in care and belonging. By conceptualizing informal educators as historical actors, this study highlights their critical role in social transformation.

papers.abstract: To support preschool educators’ integration of science in their classrooms, our project is co-designing the Early Science Hub (Hub), a professional learning resource based on promising components identified in prior work, with partner educators and curriculum/media designers. The Hub and its components are being designed to leverage technology and include educative features to make the resource widely accessible across early learning contexts. This paper details the design and iteration of one specific Hub component, the interactive simulations of science core ideas and cross cutting concepts designed to support preschool educators’ understanding of these. The session will invite participants to explore the interactive simulations and engage in a discussion to gather their insights and feedback, which can inform potential future iterations.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a case study of a teacher and researcher who worked together as part of a larger research -practice partnership. Collaborative reflection on the development and success of their work together over time highlighted several critical events in their learning process. The case describes these events as well as common themes that emerged across them and how they supported changes in the teacher’s practice. Implications for teacher learning and effective professional development are discussed.

papers.abstract: Our tool demo will explore intersections between narrative-centered learning, AI agents as inquiry scaffolds, and the interdisciplinary exploration of socioscientific issues. We will share our current design of SciStory: Pollinators, an interactive visual novel designed to support middle grades students in developing persuasive arguments to solve socioscientific problems in their community. Discussion will explore how we balance ethical issues around generative AI in our agent design, leverage co-design practices to iteratively improve collaborative game features, and draw on principles from problem-based learning to engage learners in developing solutions for complex socioscientific issues.

papers.abstract: This study explores how preservice teachers engage with artificial intelligence (AI)- powered virtual students in VR classrooms, focusing on psychological distance and construal - level theory. Using a mixed- methods approach, we analyzed interaction data from 29 participants. Findings show higher levels of abstract thinking and temporal imme diacy during teaching decisions. These results highlight how cognitive distance influences pedagogical reasoning. Insights inform the design of AI agents in immersive environments, supporting adaptive teacher learning through reflective, experience-oriented simulations.

papers.abstract: This interactive poster symposium brings together approaches to working with and studying AI that are not often explicitly connected (and are often placed in opposition to one another), those concerned with the human purposes of creativity and control. The contexts of our studies vary widely: formal education, afterschool or summer programs, community workshops, and professional performing arts. Learners, users, and scholars grapple with the ethics and challenges, as well as the potentials, of AI in their lives and in society. Putting these research projects in dialogue with one another will result in a session that fosters balance and creates a cautious yet hopeful conversation.

papers.title: From Tool to Encounter: Generative AI as a Catalyst for Ethical and Epistemic Transformation in STEM Teacher Learning
papers.authors: Sophia Jeong, Sevil Akaygun, Mutlu Şen Akbulut, Ulku Seher Budak

papers.design_stakeholders: Math Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This paper examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) reconfigures teacher learning within STEM education through a posthumanist and diffractive lens. Drawing on an empirical study involving preservice and inservice teachers engaged in AI -integrated science and mathematics classrooms, the paper reconceptualizes GenAI not as an instructional tool but as a pedagogical encounter and an active participant shaping teachers’ epistemological and ethical becomings. Using data from microteaching sessions, collaborative lesson design, and reflective narratives, the study maps how teachers negotiate distributed learning and ethical response-ability as they design and critique AI -mediated learning activities. Findings reveal three entangled processes : emergent agency in classroom dialogues, distributed learning between teachers and AI tools, and ethical reconfigurations of teacher becoming. The paper proposes an onto- epistemological framework for GenAI integration that emphasizes relationality, reflexivity, and culturally responsive practice, contributing to lea rning sciences scholarship on technology-mediated teacher education.

papers.abstract: My research explores how to support K-12 science teachers’ professional development toward equitable and justice-centered teaching. Positioning teachers and students as those who decide what matters to them in their local contexts, I leverage design-based research to co-design, test, and co-refine pedagogical tools with practitioners. Through this process, I study teacher learning by drawing upon a professional identity development lens. In my most recent work, I study how to support middle school science teachers in customizing high-quality instructional materials and investigate how curriculum customization catalyzes teacher teaching. Looking forward, I hope to explore how community-based curriculum design and customization help science teachers create equitable learning experiences for their students.

papers.title: “Both Are Useful”: Student Epistemic Navigation in a Co-Designed Science Unit about Traditional Chinese Medicine
papers.authors: Weiying Li
papers.teacher_involvement: **Involvement**: Teachers actively participated in collaborative co-design workshops, design meetings, or teacher communities with researchers to iteratively develop, test, and adapt curriculum units, assessments, and lesson plans. **Evidence**: "Future work might examine how teachers' own epistemological perspectives shift through sustained co-design, and whether extended units with more CER practice opportunities support students in reaching higher levels of epistemic integration across other culturally meaningful ph..."

papers.abstract: Science education in rural China often privileges Western epistemology, creating disconnects with students ’ community knowledge systems like Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM). This design-based research study addresses this gap through a co-designed three-lesson unit in a rural middle school in central China. The unit on Shanghuo ( 上火, internal heat) positioned TCM and Western science as complementary systems with distinct goals, reasoning processes, and evidence criteria. Using a Knowledge Integration framework, analysis of 40 eighth-graders' responses reveals how students navigated between correspondence -based and reductionist causal reasoning without devaluing community knowledge. Students shifted from binary epistemological stances ( “TCM is superstitious” ) to purposeful differentiation, recognizing when each system serves specific purposes. Three instructional routines supported this work: organizing family knowledge as analyzable data, using parallel comparison structures, and scaffolding dual justification. Findings demonstrate that rural students possess rich epistemological resources that Western -dominant curricula render invisible, offering design guidelines for culturally relevant science pedagogy.

papers.abstract: Humanizing Institutional Landscapes of Ability Differences and Learning Cathery Yeh, Erin McCloskey, Alfredo J. Artiles, Mimi Ito How can schools, universities, and community spaces construct, reinforce, or challenge how ability differences and disabilities are understood and organized in relation to race, language, and culture? This session brings together researchers working in schools, higher education, and out-of-school settings to study, reconceptualize, and redesign institutional, programmatic, and pedagogical practices. Through an engaging, dialogic format, the panelists will share stories and artifacts from four participatory design projects and explore common themes and challenges. The goal is to grapple with institutional landscapes that unevenly distribute learning opportunities, and to consider what equitable, culturally sustaining approaches to ability differences and disabilities in learning might look like. Cathery Yeh uses participatory mapping with youth, teachers, and families to capture lived experiences, decision points, and institutional boundaries shaping access, labels, and opportunities across bilingual education, special education, and mathematics, tracing patterns of exclusion and possibility to inform asset-based intervention systems. papers.abstract: In this demo, we discuss the co-design of an interactive, problem-based science supplement called Trend Trackers. Trend Trackers aims to engage middle school students with socioscientific issues that impact cities and communities all over the world. Students take up the role of a data scientist to address public health problems within the fictional city of Springfield. In this demo, we will explore a challenge in which students are asked to design a vaccination plan to reduce the rates of flu in Springfield. Students engage in interactive and immersive activities to collect wastewater samples, measure rates of flu in the community, and generate evidence through a series of wrangling, visualization, and analysis activities. Students then share their findings and collaborate with their team to co-construct a vaccination plan for Springfield.
